title: The Sharp, Organised Base
lede: Cooking feels chaotic until two things are handled — a sharp knife and mise en place. This is the precision layer everything else in the manual sits on: get it right and every later lesson runs faster, safer, and with fewer variables drifting out of range.

blocks.html: You already know this feeling from coffee: a badly-aligned burr and an unlevelled scale don't just make a worse cup — they make the whole process unreadable. You can't tell whether the shot ran fast because of grind or because of a channel. The kitchen has the same failure mode. A dull knife and an unprepared bench inject noise into everything downstream, so you can never tell whether the dish failed because of your technique or because your onion was in six different sizes.

Phase 0 removes that noise. It buys you two things before you cook a single serious dish: an edge that cuts on its own weight, and a workflow where every ingredient is prepped, weighed, and arranged before the pan gets hot. Neither is glamorous. Both are the difference between a kitchen that feels like a lab and one that feels like a fire drill.

blocks.label: Why this framing works for you
blocks.html: Sharpness and mise en place are the two variables with the highest transfer in the entire curriculum. They touch every later session. Two weeks spent here compounds across the next twelve months; skipping it taxes every dish you'll ever cook.

items.label: L1 · Functional — I cut safely and my bench is set before heat
L2 · Consistent — my dice is uniform and I can put a working edge on a knife
L3 · Optimisation — I match bevel angle, grit, and cut size to the job
L4 · Mastery — I diagnose a bad edge or a sticking pan by feel and fix it fast

blocks.html: Three subsystems, one goal: get raw material into the pan in a controlled, uniform state, then apply heat you can read. Sharpness is edge geometry. Mise en place is workstation setup. Heat control is reading thermal state. Understand each as a set of variables, not a set of rules.

Sharpness is geometry, not magic. An edge is simply where two bevels meet. When they meet at a fine line — an apex only a fraction of a micron wide — the edge concentrates your hand force onto almost no area, so it parts fibres instead of crushing them. "Dull" isn't the metal getting soft; it's the apex rounding over into a tiny cylinder. Now the same hand force is spread over a wider contact patch, pressure collapses, and the blade skates and crushes. The counter-intuitive consequence: a sharp knife is safer, because it needs less force, and less force means less slip.

blocks.html: Sharpening removes metal to re-form the apex; honing only realigns it. Under use, a thin edge rolls over to one side long before it truly wears away — that's why a knife feels dull after a week but doesn't actually need a stone. A honing steel (or ceramic rod) pushes that rolled edge back into line. A whetstone is different in kind: it abrades steel off both bevels until they meet again at a fresh apex. Confusing the two is the single most common beginner error — people "sharpen" on a steel forever and wonder why nothing improves.

blocks.html: Mise en place is workstation setup. It is the exact analog of dosing, levelling, and lining up your portafilter, tamper, and cup before you pull the shot. Once the pan is at temperature you have seconds, not minutes — garlic goes from raw to burnt in under 30 s in a hot pan. Chopping while cooking guarantees something scorches. So all cutting, weighing, and measuring happens first, arranged in the order you'll add it. The bench becomes a queue; cooking becomes execution.

Heat control is reading thermal state. Heat reaches food three ways, and knowing which one dominates tells you what to expect. Conduction (metal-to-food, a searing pan) is fast and intense — this is where browning lives. Convection (hot air or oil moving) is gentler and more even — ovens, deep-frying. Radiation (glowing element, grill, broiler) cooks the facing surface hard. A pan has thermal mass: it stores energy, so a properly preheated heavy pan barely dips when cold food lands, while a thin cold pan crashes and the food steams in its own juices instead of searing.

items.title: The apex & bevel angle
items.html: What: the edge is two bevels meeting at a line; the included angle sets the trade-off. Why it matters: a thinner angle (Japanese ~10–15°/side) cuts finer but chips; a wider angle (Western ~15–20°/side) is tougher but drags more. Common mistake: putting a delicate 12° edge on a knife you use to hack squash — it chips within a week.

items.title: The burr
items.html: What: a thin flap of displaced steel that forms on the opposite side when your grinding has finally reached the apex. Why it matters: it's your only reliable signal that a bevel is fully sharpened, edge-to-edge. Common mistake: stopping before the burr forms (edge still rounded) or leaving the burr on (feels sharp, folds over instantly in use).

items.title: Grit progression
items.html: What: coarse stones cut fast and rough; fine stones refine and polish. Why it matters: ~400 grit sets the bevel and raises a burr fast; ~1000 sharpens a working edge; ~3000–6000 refines to a push-cutting polish. Common mistake: starting too fine — spending 20 minutes at 1000 grit trying to fix damage that a 400 would remove in two.

items.title: The claw & pinch grip
items.html: What: guiding hand curls fingertips under (knuckles guide the blade); knife hand pinches the blade just ahead of the handle. Why it matters: the claw makes it geometrically impossible to cut a fingertip, and the pinch gives blade control instead of wrist-flail. Common mistake: gripping the handle like a hammer — no control, and fingers extended into the path.

items.title: Slice, don't press
items.html: What: cutting is a draw or push stroke, letting the edge's length do the work, not a guillotine chop straight down. Why it matters: a slicing motion needs a fraction of the downward force and severs cleanly instead of crushing (which is why tomatoes explode under a dull, pressed blade). Common mistake: pushing straight down and bruising herbs into a black paste.

items.title: Uniform size = even cooking
items.html: What: every piece the same dimension so they hit doneness together. Why it matters: a pan of mixed 3 mm and 12 mm onion gives you burnt shreds and raw chunks in one bite — the real reason chefs obsess over knife cuts. Common mistake: thinking uniformity is aesthetic. It's thermal.

blocks.label: The variable that matters most here
blocks.html: Size uniformity is a heat-control variable in disguise. Cook time is set by the largest piece; overcook is set by the smallest. Tighten the spread and both problems shrink at once.
Buy few things, buy them once, and spend the saved money on a practice knife you're allowed to wreck. The whole starter kit costs less than one mid-range espresso grinder.

blocks.title: Starter kit — necessary

rows.value: One good all-rounder. Full tang, comfortable pinch grip. This does 90% of all cutting. Budget the most here.
Large end-grain or edge-grain wood, or thick HDPE plastic. Big enough to hold prep without crowding. Kind to your edge.
0.1 g resolution, ≥3 kg capacity, tare button. Weight beats volume for reproducibility — same reason you dose by mass in coffee.
Fast (<4 s) thermocouple-style probe. Turns "is it done?" from guesswork into a number.
One combination stone, ~1000/6000 grit, plus a cheap practice knife to learn on before touching the good one.

blocks.title: Optional — buy later, when a real need appears

rows.value: Handy for small in-hand work (hulling, peeling). The chef's knife covers most of it at first.
Realigns the edge between sharpenings. Useful, not urgent — a fresh stone edge lasts weeks.
Add when you need to reset a damaged or badly-angled bevel. The 1000 side handles routine sharpening.
Moves prepped piles cleanly into bowls — small mise en place quality-of-life win.

blocks.title: Waste of money — actively skip

rows.value: You pay for 12 mediocre knives to get one usable one, plus a santoku and 8 steak knives you'll never sharpen. Buy the single good chef's knife instead.
Fixed carbide wheels grind a crude, over-wide bevel and tear metal. Fast, satisfying, and they shorten your knife's life. Skip.
Same problem, less power. They set a random angle and gouge the apex. A stone costs the same and teaches you the mechanism.
The skill you're building is the tool. Every gadget is a thing to store, clean, and not learn from.

blocks.label: What beginners get wrong buying tools
blocks.html: Spending on breadth (a huge set) instead of depth (one good knife you maintain). A single sharp 8" chef's knife outperforms a $300 block of dull ones on day one and every day after.

blocks.html:
1. Prep. Stabilise the board — a damp paper towel or thin silicone mat underneath kills all slide. An unstable board is the number-one cause of cuts. Wipe the handle and your hands dry.
  2. Prep. Create a flat. Never cut on a round surface — halve the onion, potato, or carrot first and set it cut-side down so it can't roll. Stability before speed, always.
  3. Execute. Pinch the blade, claw the food, and let the edge slice — push forward and down, or draw back and down, riding your knuckles as a guide rail. Never press straight down.
  4. Execute. Keep the tip on the board for chopping (a pivot); lift only the heel. Move the food into the blade with the claw; don't chase it with the knife.
  5. Evaluate. If pieces vary in size, you're cutting from feel, not from a reference face. If the blade skates, it's dull or you're pressing not slicing.
  6. Correct. Slow down to 60% speed until the size is uniform, then rebuild pace. Speed is a by-product of consistency, never a target you chase directly. And never — ever — try to catch a falling knife. Step back, let it drop, pick it up.

blocks.label: L2 Consistent — a working edge on demand

blocks.html:
1. Prep. Soak a soaking-type whetstone 5–10 min until bubbles stop. Set it on a non-slip base. Decide your angle: lay the blade flat, lift the spine ~2 coins high (~15°) for a Japanese knife, ~3 coins (~20°) for a Western one. Consistency of angle beats the exact number.
  2. Execute. On the coarse/1000 side, push the edge across the stone as if shaving a thin layer off the surface, keeping the angle locked. Cover the whole edge, heel to tip, ~10–15 passes per section. Keep the stone wet.
  3. Evaluate. Feel for the burr: run a fingertip off the edge (never along it) on the opposite side. A tiny catching flap the full length of the blade means that side is done. No burr = apex not reached; keep going.
  4. Execute. Flip and repeat on the other side until the burr forms on the first side. Then alternate light passes to work the burr thinner.
  5. Evaluate. Move to the 3000–6000 side; a few light alternating passes refine the apex and knock the burr off. Strop on the edge of the board or denim to remove the last of it.
  6. Correct. Test: the edge should catch and cut printer paper cleanly, or shave arm hair with no pressure. If it tears paper, the burr is still on or the apex isn't met — return to 1000.

blocks.problem: Diced onion falls apart into a mess

fields.detail: You cut off the root end (the natural clamp), or your horizontal/vertical cuts didn't go through the same layers.
Look at the onion half: is the root intact and pointing at your guiding hand?
Halve pole-to-pole, leave the root end attached, make vertical cuts toward (not through) the root, then cross-cut. The root holds all the layers together until the last second.

blocks.problem: Dice is uneven — burnt shreds and raw chunks in the pan

fields.detail: Inconsistent spacing because you're eyeballing, or a dull knife wandering off line.
Lay ten pieces in a row. If they range more than ~2× smallest-to-largest, that's the problem.
Use the previous cut face as your ruler — space each cut to match it. Slow to 60% pace. Sharpen the knife; a wandering blade can't be precise no matter how steady your hand.

blocks.problem: Knife won't get sharp on the stone

fields.detail: Inconsistent angle (rocking your wrist), stone dried out, or you stopped before raising a burr.
Colour the bevel with marker and take two passes — if the marker is removed unevenly, your angle is wandering.

Lock the angle with your whole arm, not your wrist. Keep the stone flooded. Grind one side until a full-length burr appears — no burr means the apex isn't reached yet, so nothing you do downstream will sharpen it.

blocks.problem: Burr won't form no matter how long I grind

fields.detail: Angle too low (spine dropping, so you polish the shoulder not the apex), or the stone is glazed/too fine to cut.
Marker test again: if only the top of the bevel loses ink and the very edge keeps it, you're grinding above the apex.
Raise the spine slightly and commit to the angle. Switch to a coarser (~400) stone to actually remove metal; refresh a glazed stone by rubbing with a coarse plate or a second stone.

blocks.problem: Food sticks and tears in the pan

fields.detail: Pan not hot enough (proteins bond to cool metal), too little/too-cold oil, or you moved the food before the crust released.
Water-drop test: flick a few drops in. If they sizzle and vanish, too cool. If they bead and skate like mercury (Leidenfrost), it's hot enough.
Preheat the empty pan, add oil, wait for it to shimmer, then add food and leave it. A properly seared surface releases itself — sticking is the food telling you it isn't done yet.

blocks.html: Change exactly one variable. Everything else held constant. This is how you build intuition you can trust instead of folklore you repeat.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E1 — sharp vs dull

fields.detail: Feel, directly, that sharp is safer and cleaner — not just "nicer".
Same onion variety, same size, same grip, same board.
One freshly-sharpened knife vs one deliberately dulled (drag the edge across a ceramic mug base a few times).
The dull knife needs 3–5× the downward force, crushes cells (more tears, weeping onion), and slips more. The sharp knife glides on its own weight.
Force required, how much the onion weeps, whether the blade skates off the skin, cleanliness of the cut faces.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E2 — board stability

fields.detail: Quantify how much a stable board matters for control and safety.
Same knife, same carrot, same cutting speed.
Board sitting bare on the counter vs board on a damp towel/silicone mat.
The bare board creeps and micro-slides on each stroke; the damped board is dead-still, and your cuts get instantly more uniform because the target isn't moving.
Board movement per stroke, size consistency of the pieces, how tense your guiding hand is.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E3 — pan preheat & the water-drop test

fields.detail: See thermal mass and Leidenfrost with your own eyes, then link it to sticking.
Same pan, same burner setting, same amount of water/oil, same food.
Cold pan (food in immediately) vs pan preheated ~2–3 min first.
Cold pan: water sizzles flat and food glues down and steams grey. Hot pan: water beads and dances (drops surviving on their own vapour ≈ 160 °C+ / 320 °F+), food sears and releases cleanly.
Droplet behaviour, whether food sticks, colour and crust development, how far the pan temperature dips when food lands.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E4 — press vs slice on a tomato

fields.detail: Prove that motion, not just sharpness, determines a clean cut.
Same knife (freshly sharp), same tomato, same slice thickness target.
Straight-down press vs a single long drawing stroke.
The press crushes the skin and squeezes out seeds and juice; the draw stroke parts the skin with almost no force and leaves an intact slice.
Skin resistance, juice loss, cleanliness of the cut face.

blocks.html: Short, repeatable, measurable. Do one or two per session as a warm-up before real cooking. The point is reps against a clear success criterion, not finishing a dish.

blocks.title: Uniform onion dice

fields.detail: A bowl of ~5 mm dice where pieces are within ±1 mm of each other.
Beginner
2–3 onions, sharp chef's knife, stable board.
Halve pole-to-pole, root intact → vertical cuts toward the root → horizontal cut(s) → cross-cut into dice. Use each prior face as the ruler for the next.
Lay ten random pieces in a row: max/min size ratio under ~1.5. Root end left as a clean handle.
Falls apart (root removed) · uneven (eyeballing spacing) · sliding onion (unstable board).
Drop to 60% speed until uniform, then rebuild pace. Sharpen if the blade wanders.

blocks.title: Paper-thin garlic slices

fields.detail: Translucent slices ~1 mm thick, even enough to fry without some burning first.
Beginner
A head of garlic, sharp knife.
Flatten a clove face for stability, claw grip, draw the blade through with light strokes — let sharpness do the work.
Slices you can nearly see through, consistent thickness; a test batch fries to gold evenly with no black pieces.
Wedge-shaped slices (angled blade) · crushed clove (pressing) · uneven fry (thickness spread).
Sharpen; this drill exposes a dull edge instantly. Focus on a consistent knuckle-guide height.

blocks.title: Herb chopping without bruising

fields.detail: Finely chopped parsley/coriander that stays green, not a wet black paste.
Beginner–Intermediate
Bunch of soft herbs, very sharp knife, dry board.
Dry the herbs well, gather into a tight pile, rock-chop with the tip anchored, re-gathering — but chop few times, not many. Slice, never mash.
Bright green herb, dry board (no green smear = you sliced, not crushed), even fineness.
Black paste (dull knife or over-chopping) · wet smear (herbs not dried, or pressing).
Sharpen and chop fewer strokes. If the board turns green, that's cell juice — you crushed it.

blocks.title: Sharpen a cheap knife to paper-cutting

fields.detail: Take a blunt practice knife to an edge that slices printer paper cleanly and shaves arm hair.
Intermediate
Cheap knife (never the good one, first few times), combination whetstone, marker.
Marker the bevel → set angle → grind one side to a full-length burr → flip → refine on the fine side → strop off the burr.
Clean paper cut with zero tearing; hairs pop off forearm; marker removed evenly right to the apex.
No burr (angle too low / stone too fine) · edge tears paper (burr still attached) · wavy edge (wandering angle).
Use the marker test every session until your angle is repeatable. Only then graduate to your real knife.

blocks.title: Timed mise en place: sofrito base

fields.detail: Prep a full aromatic base — diced onion, sliced garlic, chopped herbs, measured oil and salt — all bowled and lined up in cooking order before any heat.
Dice, slice, chop, mise en place discipline, working from a queue.
Everything staged so the actual cook is 3–4 minutes of pure execution with nothing left to chop.
Did you have to stop and cut anything after the pan was hot? If yes, your mise wasn't complete. Nothing scorched while you scrambled = pass.

blocks.title: Sear something with a read pan

fields.detail: Sear a protein (chicken thigh, a firm mushroom, or tofu) using the water-drop test to judge readiness, and build fond.
Preheating & thermal mass, Leidenfrost reading, patience (leaving food to release), recognising fond.
A deep-brown crust that releases itself, and browned bits (fond) stuck to the pan — the flavour base for a future sauce.
Even golden-brown crust, no grey steaming, food released without tearing. Fond is browned (flavour) not black (bitter).

blocks.title: Restore and maintain your good knife

fields.detail: Full sharpen of your primary chef's knife — correct angle set, burr raised and removed, polished — then establish a maintenance rhythm.
Angle consistency, grit progression, burr control, honing-vs-sharpening judgement.
A knife that push-cuts paper and falls through an onion, plus a written rule for when you hone vs when you go back to the stone.
Clean paper slice, shaving-sharp, no chips. You can state — from feel — whether an edge needs honing or sharpening.

blocks.html: Train your eye on what a good edge and a good cut actually look like before you try to make one.

blocks.look: Look for: a consistent bevel meeting at a clean, unbroken apex line — no reflective flat band along the very edge (a reflective line = a rounded, dull apex catching light).

blocks.query: burr on knife edge sharpening macro
blocks.look: Look for: the thin flap of steel bent over to one side. This is the signal you're chasing on the stone — recognise it visually so you trust the finger test.

blocks.query: brunoise dice julienne knife cuts comparison
blocks.look: Look for: how uniform professional cuts are, and the named size steps (see table below). Notice they're all cubes/sticks of one dimension — that's the standard you're calibrating against.

blocks.query: Leidenfrost effect water droplet hot pan
blocks.look: Look for: droplets balling up and skating on their own vapour cushion. This is the visual signal your pan is sear-ready.

blocks.label: Knowledge check — understanding, not recall
blocks.html: Answer these in your own words; if you can, you own the mechanism:

1. Q. Explain, in terms of force and contact area, why a sharper knife is safer — not just more effective.
  2. Q. A friend "sharpens" their knife on a honing steel every day and it's still dull after a month. What's actually happening, and what do they need instead?
  3. Q. Why does uneven dice cause both burnt and raw pieces in the same pan? Frame it as a heat-control problem, not an aesthetic one.
  4. Q. Your food is steaming grey and sticking instead of browning. Name three variables you'd check, and the test you'd run to decide the pan is ready.
  5. Q. What is a burr, why do you want to raise one on the stone, and why must it be gone before you use the knife?

blocks.label: Practical challenge
blocks.html: Cold start to plated in one continuous run: sharpen a knife to paper-cutting, then dice one onion to within ±1 mm uniformity, slice garlic paper-thin, chop a handful of herbs bright and dry, and sear one item in a properly-read pan until it releases itself with visible fond. No stopping to cut after the pan is hot — that's the mise en place half of the test.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.html: Where did the process feel unreadable — a moment you couldn't tell why something went wrong? That's your next variable to isolate. Which single change (sharper edge, more complete mise, hotter pan) removed the most chaos? Note it; that's the leverage point you'll return to in Module 01 when the food gets less forgiving.
